text: Two men have hated each other for years, and their children have just given the hatred something to do. The fathers do not hedge: they say they would go as far as killing before accepting the match, and the film takes that at face value rather than as bluster. Filmfare named it Best Film. Mansoor Khan runs the courtship and the feud on a single clock for 162 minutes, so every hour Raj and Rashmi spend together is an hour charged to someone at home. The interest is less in whether the two of them hold than in how completely a quarrel can be handed down - they had no part in starting it and are expected to carry it regardless. Declining an inheritance of that kind takes more nerve than romance usually asks for.

God turns up as a mild old man and asks the assistant manager of a grocery store to speak for him. Carl Reiner keeps that at the scale it deserves: 98 minutes, no thunder, a man with a job to get back to who has been handed an assignment he cannot show to anyone. Fantasy usually solves this by making the messenger exceptional in some way. Here the whole comedy depends on him not being. The adapted screenplay took an Academy Award, and the writing shows in what it withholds - the film neither mocks the premise nor solemnises it, and the real pressure is procedural: whom he tells, in what order, and what those people will accept in place of proof of a conversation that had no witnesses.

The trip has been planned for years, and retirement finally makes it possible - chiefly, it makes possible the discovery that husband and wife were planning different trips. He built automobiles and has stopped. She has been waiting for whatever comes after, and the two versions of afterward do not match. William Wyler keeps everything at conversation level across 101 minutes and lets the trouble surface as preference rather than accusation: what to look at, whom to sit with, how long to stay, whether to go back at all. Neither of them behaves badly. That is the difficulty - a marriage can come apart on nothing worse than taste, and taste is the one thing neither party can concede without agreeing to be somebody else for the rest of their life.

The plan is modest - get to New York, make the interview, go home - and the plan is the first thing to go. Arthur Hiller's city does not menace the couple so much as process them: New York assumes competence, and they have come in from a small town without the local knowledge that would let them argue with it. 98 minutes of escalation, each setback growing out of the wreckage of the last one. The comedy holds because the two of them stay decent; they keep behaving as though a complaint will be recorded somewhere and someone will answer for it. The Writers Guild singled out the screenplay, and the construction is the joke - an ordinary itinerary taken apart in the exact order an itinerary comes.

Marguerite Gautier is paid for her company, and nobody in the room pretends otherwise. George Cukor lays 1847 Paris out as a business with good manners: gambling rooms, late suppers, men of means setting the terms, women expected to enjoy the arrangement convincingly. Then Armand Duval, and a romance that will cost her more than it costs him. The 109 minutes are less about passion than about arithmetic - what a season of sincerity is worth to a woman whose income is her charm, and what she would have to stop doing in order to have one. The lead performance took the Academy Award for Best Actress. Everything else in these rooms carries a price and everyone present knows it; the film is about the one thing that does not, and about who can afford it.

It is 1941, and France has still not left the nineteenth century: coal, steam, and an emperor named Napoleon V. The reason is also the plot, since a world where invention stopped is a world somebody has been holding still, and Avril's parents, scientists, are among the missing. Animation lets a premise like that be built rather than argued - 106 minutes of a France that never received the twentieth century, everything in it heavier and slower and louder than it ought to be, and a teenage girl moving through it in search of two particular people rather than a cause. It took the Cristal at Annecy. The chase works because the machinery does: the film has worked out how a country kept at half power would look, then sends a daughter running through it.

An unhappy wife says she wants to dance, and the guide who is paid to be agreeable tells her yes. Vijay Anand gives that exchange 183 minutes, which is room enough for encouragement to turn into a career, a career into an income, and the man who supplied the encouragement to develop a relationship to her success that he had not planned on. His trade is the key to him: a guide knows a place well enough to hand it to strangers, and lives on the goodwill of people who are leaving. India submitted the film to the Academy Awards. What holds it upright over three hours is that her ambition is treated as hers - not a subplot inside his life, but the thing that reorganises both of them without asking his permission first.

Raja drives a taxi, Aarti's family has money, and the marriage happens over her parents' objection. Dharmesh Darshan then spends most of 177 minutes on what a wedding does not settle: a household deciding, daily, whether to absorb the man it did not choose, and a stepmother whose project is the rift itself. Melodrama at this length is often accused of stalling. The length is the argument - distrust is not an event but a long accumulation of small deferrals, and there is time here to watch them add up. Filmfare gave it Best Film. The money never softens into metaphor either: the difference between the two of them stays a matter of who pays, who is expected to be grateful for it, and how quickly a favour turns into a debt.

A father leaves the village to find work in the city, and his son goes after him. Alê Abreu made the journey out of several drawing techniques at once, and the switching is not decoration: what the boy meets on the road, engines built like insects and figures he has no word for, arrives as a different kind of mark each time, because he has nothing to match any of it against. Brazil, 2013, eighty minutes. Underneath the fable is a question about work - where it goes, who follows it, and what is left in a village once the wages have gone on ahead of the people. The Cristal at Annecy went to it. It is made for children and does not lie to them about the machines.

Bob and Carol come back from a group therapy session with a new commitment to candour and spend it immediately on their closest friends. Ted and Alice are too well mannered to refuse the counselling. That politeness is the engine: four adults in 1969, none of them able to decline a fashionable idea without looking small, talking themselves by degrees into territory none of them chose. Paul Mazursky lets dialogue carry all 105 minutes, and the comedy is one of nerve - the distance between what people will agree to out loud and what they actually intend to do about it. The tension among the four predates the therapy; the session only handed them a vocabulary for it, and a reason to keep the subject open.

Summer 1939, in a village where Polish, Ukrainian and Jewish families live along the same road. Zosia loves Petro; her father marries her instead to Skiba, a widower with land, because that is the arrangement available to him. Then the army takes her husband for the war with Germany, and she is left keeping a house that is not hers among neighbours who are about to be asked what they are before they are asked anything else. Wojtek Smarzowski works at ground level for 150 minutes - the match, the property, the terms agreed over her head - and the history reaches the village as a change in how people greet one another. The first hour is spent making the households known, which is the only way the rest can register as anything but distance.

A rainbow suit carries a ten-year-old through the air, and on his first flight he loses control of it. Arco comes down in 2075, which from where he started is the remote past, and is found by Iris, a girl his own age who decides to get him home and will try anything to manage it. Ugo Bienvenu holds this to 89 minutes and to a scale of problem a child recognises: a stranger who cannot be explained to any adult, a way back that nobody knows how to build, a secret that gets heavier the longer it is kept. His own century needs almost no explaining for the trouble to work - it is enough that everything here is older and cruder than what he left. The rescue stays a child's undertaking, run on a child's resources.
